words.sense: Having meaningful content, effect, or value rather than being merely superficial.
misconceptions: Treats length or size as proof of meaningful content.
Treats thoughtful content as necessarily large in quantity.

words.sense: Large or considerable in size, amount, or extent.
misconceptions: Treats length or size as proof of meaningful content.
Treats thoughtful content as necessarily large in quantity.

semantic_axes.description: Substantive emphasizes meaningful content or effect, whereas substantial emphasizes considerable magnitude or extent.

edges.boundary_rule: Substantive emphasizes meaningful content or effect, whereas substantial emphasizes considerable magnitude or extent.

misconceptions.M1: Treats length or size as proof of meaningful content.
misconceptions.M2: Treats thoughtful content as necessarily large in quantity.
misconceptions.M3: Ignores the original basis when an impressive distraction appears.

chains.frame: Which word best describes Amina’s revision to her essay?

beats.text: Amina replaced broad claims with comparisons and evidence that changed her conclusion.
beats.reason: The first beat supplies the deciding evidence: evidence changed the actual argument.

beats.text: Her new version was also shorter than the draft she handed in last week.
beats.reason: A shorter text can still make a meaningful intellectual change.

chains.feedback_short: Evidence changed the actual argument — the later detail does not change that distinction.
chains.feedback_deep: Substantive means having meaningful content, effect, or value rather than being merely superficial. Substantial means large or considerable in size, amount, or extent. Here, evidence changed the actual argument; a shorter text can still make a meaningful intellectual change.
chains.contrast_rule: Substantive emphasizes meaningful content or effect, whereas substantial emphasizes considerable magnitude or extent.
